state.misconception_label: Has used slant height and base to find area of a triangle rather than perpendicular height and base

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: How would you calculate the area of this triangle? ![A triangle, base 12m. All three sides are equal.](). I got \( \frac{12 \times 12}{2} \) because I added the side lengths instead of multiplying.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of the triangle as a roof of a house with a slanted roof. To find the area of the triangle, you need to use the perpendicular height, which is like the height of the house from the ground to the top of the roof. So, instead of using the slant height, focus on finding the perpendicular height and multiply it by the base to get the correct area.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so the perpendicular height is like going straight up from the ground, not along the slanted roof? So for this triangle, I need to find that straight-up height first before I multiply it by the base of 12m?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Yes, exactly! Think of it like measuring how tall the house is from the ground to the top, rather than along the slanted roof. Once you find that perpendicular height, you can multiply it by the base of the triangle to calculate the correct area. Keep focusing on finding that straight-up height!

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: So like, I need to measure straight up from the base to the top point of the triangle, not along the slanted side? But how do I actually find that height - do I need to measure it, or can I work it out from the side lengths somehow?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the slant vs. perpendicular height misconception with a clear analogy, but provides direct explanations rather than prompting student reasoning, though the student does show clear conceptual progress by Turn 4 when asking how to calculate the height.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses a concrete real-world analogy (house with a slanted roof) to explain the abstract concept of perpendicular height in triangle area calculation, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
